claims.text: Controlled thermal aging drives a metastable-to-intermetallic transformation in the Mg-containing lightweight HEA.
The metastable-to-intermetallic transformation degrades corrosion resistance.
The metastable-to-intermetallic transformation degrades high-temperature oxidation resistance.
The as-quenched metastable solid-solution state has superior environmental resistance relative to the aged state.
Systematic annealing induces discrete intermetallic precipitation.
Intermetallic precipitation disrupts the continuity of the protective surface oxide film.
The initial material is a non-equilibrium Mg-bearing alloy containing a metastable solid solution.
As-quenched samples are to be used as controls for systematically annealed samples.
The selected annealing temperatures and durations will be sufficient to initiate diffusion-controlled nucleation and growth of intermetallic compounds.
The structural mediator is nucleation and growth of discrete intermetallic precipitates within the matrix.
Thermally activated diffusion at service-simulated temperatures forms intermetallic phases from the metastable solid solution.
Intermetallic precipitation impairs formation and maintenance of a protective oxide layer.
Aged samples will develop and coarsen intermetallic precipitates with increasing aging time.
Aged samples will exhibit a measurable decrease in corrosion resistance relative to as-quenched controls.
Aged samples will exhibit a measurable decrease in high-temperature oxidation resistance relative to as-quenched controls.
The initial as-quenched state has a uniform solid-solution microstructure.
The initial as-quenched state has high corrosion and oxidation resistance.
Similar Mg-containing alloy systems show a general tendency toward intermetallic formation.
The exact transformation kinetics and critical precipitate density for degradation are not yet quantified.
Observation of intermetallic growth without degradation of either corrosion or oxidation resistance would falsify the proposed mechanistic link.
